1.0.0.en: Bishops: in Greek the word means overseers of the churches. It refers to the bishops and the priests, their assistants, who are responsible for the care of the people.

1.0.1.en: Deacons: in Syriac, servants. They are the helpers in the care of the people together with the bishops and the priests. St. Paul joins the name of his disciple Timothy to his own without distinction or discrimination, making his disciple equal to himself, which shows his humility. Paul feels that he belongs to God, for He bought him with His precious blood, so that he became His servant, and the servant has only to obey his master. He refrained from going to places where he wished to go, and went in obedience to God's command in the vision in which the man of Macedonia appeared to him saying, "Come over to us and help us" (Acts 16:9). He sends his greeting to the saints in Christ Jesus who are believers, and singles out the shepherds because they represent all the people whom they shepherd.

1.1.0.en: Grace was the greeting with which the Greeks began their letters, and peace is the Hebrew greeting with which the Jews greeted one another. Therefore St. Paul was accustomed always to join these two greetings in his letters, to show that Christ is for everyone.

1.1.1.en: Submission to the will of God gives a person rest. So accept His will in your life in the difficult matters that come upon you, or those that run contrary to your plans, confident that it is better than what you would have arranged, and Christ will bear the responsibility for you and give you peace.

1.2.s.en: (2) Paul's love and his prayers for them

1.2.0.en: St. Paul thanks God whenever he remembers the people of Philippi, because of their faith and their love.

1.2.1.en: May we thank God for the many blessings with which He has favored us. This is what the Church teaches us, for she begins her prayers on all occasions with the prayer of thanksgiving, because thanksgiving makes you aware of the grace of God that is with you. So be confident in yourself, upheld by God, and rejoice in His work in you.

1.3.0.en: St. Paul remembers them always whenever he prays, mingling thanksgiving with supplication.

1.3.1.en: He prays with joy despite the harassment of those who oppose him and the hardship of prison and chains, because he feels the presence of Christ with him and rejoices in the growth of the ministry although he is bound in prison.

1.3.2.en: May we not stand before God every time only to ask and ask and forget to thank Him, and when we ask, may we not forget to ask on behalf of others.

1.4.0.en: St. Paul prays and thanks God for the love of the people of Philippi, who contributed to the needs of the preaching of the Gospel from the first day on which they were brought to faith until this time in which he writes his letter as a prisoner, a period of nearly ten years.

1.5.0.en: Paul is confident that God, who gave them the grace of giving, is able to establish them in this virtue until His Second Coming, that they may rejoice with Him in heaven.

1.6.0.en: St. Paul shows his fatherhood not only in praying for the people of Philippi, but in his love and his constant feeling for them, even in the midst of tribulations, while in the chains of prison and while preaching and defending the Gospel. He praises them as his partners in the grace of preaching, because they helped him in his material needs, so that they have the reward of preaching just as he does.

1.7.0.en: St. Paul calls God to witness to the truth of his words concerning the tender feelings and affections he bears for them all. These are not feelings of human love but spiritual love, which he received from Christ, who loved them with a deep love (bowels), so that He gave Himself for them.

1.8.0.en: The Apostle prays always for them that their love for God and for people may grow more and more, a love founded on knowledge and spiritual understanding.

1.9.0.en: True love for God grants a person an enlightened mind and the virtue of discerning between conflicting matters, so that he chooses what is good among them and leaves what is not good. Thus we do not halt between two sides, nor do we sow any confusion of thought in the holy Church, and we continue in our faithfulness to the Gospel and avoid stumbling until the day of Christ's Second Coming.

1.10.0.en: The righteous Christian must bear fruit, and the fruit of righteousness is good works. But let us know that this fruit is not from ourselves but is from God and to the glory of God.

1.11.0.en: The Apostle reassures the people of Philippi that his imprisonment did not hinder the preaching of the Gospel, but on the contrary was a cause of the advance of preaching in Rome.

1.12.0.en: It has now become known to everyone that his chains are not because of any offense he committed, but because of his faith in Christ. The preaching has spread, not only in the governor's palace through each soldier of the imperial guard whose hand was bound to the hand of St. Paul during his watch, but in all other places as well.

1.13.0.en: When the brethren saw Paul's preaching while a prisoner and saw his joy in the midst of sufferings, they were filled with zeal and fervor, and preached the name of Christ without fear.

1.14.0.en: There were some who preached Christ to the people while their hearts overflowed with envy of Paul and jealousy toward him, hoping to gain a better renown and reputation than his. But there are others who are sincere in their preaching, who do it out of love and a genuine desire for the salvation of souls.

1.15.0.en: There are those who preach for personal gain and selfish ambition, and this is the correct translation of the original Greek word rendered in Arabic "contention." They aim to obtain people's esteem and the glorifying of themselves. These are insincere in their preaching and their proclaiming of Christ, and their aim is to trouble St. Paul and fight him, and they wish to torment him with a mental torment more severe than the torment of the iron chains with which he is bound in his prison.

1.16.0.en: But the others teach with the mind of Christ, and they are impelled to preach by love for God and for people, knowing that St. Paul is appointed by divine providence to spread the Gospel.

1.17.0.en: Here St. Paul shows his attitude toward all of these, and asks, saying: What then ... Then he answers that whether the preaching is out of self-glorification or out of pure love for God, he rejoices in every case in the spread of the joyful message and the spread of the name of Christ, and he rejoices also because God will turn evil into good.

1.17.1.en: Accept other opinions that oppose yours if they are useful and constructive. The difference of opinions should not disturb you; rather encourage it, since it means that others are concerned about the matter, and this is not against your dignity. And if you are disturbed, know that there is pride within you and that you need repentance.

1.18.0.en: The Apostle knows with certainty that every persecution turns into a credit that secures for him the salvation to which he looks forward upon entering eternity, through their prayers and the support of the Holy Spirit, that is, the Spirit of Jesus Christ.

1.19.0.en: All that he awaits and hopes for is that he not fail in his preaching but boldly proclaim his witness to Christ at all times, so that the name of Christ may be glorified through his bodily sufferings and his chains, and even his death and martyrdom will proclaim the life of Christ in him.

1.20.0.en: For me to live is Christ: this phrase shows us the Apostle's mind, for he sees his life hidden in Christ, that is, Christ for him is the center of life and the center of thought and is everything. To die is gain: the Apostle looks at death as a means of departing from the world to blessed eternity, and a departure from the prison of the body to the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

1.21.0.en: The work of preaching and the abundant fruit that the Apostle gathers into the fold of Christ leave him in perplexity as to which to choose: life, where he serves his brethren, or death, where he will be with Christ?

1.22.0.en: These two desires dominate him: the desire to depart from the captivity of the body to the Kingdom of Heaven, where he will be with Christ all the time, enjoying life with Him, a spiritual enjoyment that no other enjoyment equals.

1.23.0.en: But for their good and their spiritual benefit and their progress in the spiritual life, it is more necessary that he remain in the flesh with them.

1.24.0.en: He is confident that his remaining in the flesh fulfills the divine will, because it is necessary for their progress and their joy in the faith in Christ.

1.25.0.en: Your rejoicing in Christ Jesus: your glorifying of God.

1.25.1.en: His remaining in the flesh increases their glorifying of the Lord. They will also rejoice at his return to them and his presence in their midst in fullness of blessing and grace after his release from prison.

1.25.2.en: How beautiful it is that you make heaven your only goal, and if you look to the earth you seek your salvation and the salvation of those around you, preparing for the Kingdom every day. Then you will experience the presence of God with you and receive the earnest of the Kingdom, which increases your longing for it until you depart toward it. And if you are occupied with the goals of the world, such as money, position, relationships and various lusts, may you repent and return quickly to your goal.

1.26.0.en: Only: here it means that what he will now say to them as a commandment is the conclusion of the whole matter.

1.26.1.en: Paul asks them to live in a manner worthy of and consistent with the commandments of the Gospel, so that whether he comes to them or hears of them during his absence, he may find that they stand firm as members of one body, that is, the body of Christ, and strive together in unity for the spread of the principles of the Gospel among everyone.

1.27.0.en: Not being afraid of the attacks of the enemy of good, however great the strength of his helpers, for their steadfastness in the faith is a strong proof of their being qualified, by grace, for salvation and for the eternal inheritance; whereas the persecution of the children of God by their opponents is a testimony of their condemnation, which will lead them to eternal destruction.

1.28.0.en: Steadfastness in the faith and spiritual striving must result in persecution and suffering. And suffering in the Christian view is a gift from God and not a punishment, and it is a sign of love and holy fellowship, behind which is a crown of glory, for suffering is linked to the Kingdom.

1.29.0.en: You are members with me in the one body; you must strive as I have striven, as you saw in my own person and now hear that I continue in it. For this is the fellowship of sufferings that will lead us to the fellowship of glory with our good Savior.

1.29.1.en: Accept the sufferings that come upon you for the sake of Christ, who bore all sufferings for you on the Cross, and you will experience His presence with you and rejoice in His consolations, and this will move you to love toil for His sake, not only in worship but in every service.

2.0.0.en: Comfort: consolation and solace, as it is said in (Col 4:11). St. Paul declares that the aim of all preaching is to proclaim Christ the Savior, and the aim of all service, consolation and support of others is love and not any personal purposes.

2.0.1.en: And the fellowship among believers has as its aim unity in the Holy Spirit and not any interests, and likewise deep feelings of love and compassion toward others have as their aim unity in the body of Christ. In sum, St. Paul calls all believers to unity in Christ and in love for Him through the Holy Spirit.

2.1.0.en: The Apostle declares that his joy will not be complete unless he is assured that they are of one mind and live in love with one purpose, and that their aim is one for all of them, namely Christ and good works.

2.2.1.en: If every member of the community had his own thoughts and his own opinion which he tried to impose on others, factions would arise which must end in division. So pride and working for self-glory are rejected in the work of the Gospel, and humility is the healing remedy, so that we give others honor and esteem and regard them as better than ourselves.

2.2.2.en: Did not the Apostle himself give us an example when he counted himself the last of all and like one born out of due time (1 Cor 15:8)?!

2.3.0.en: A person often concentrates his effort and his concerns on himself, heedless of his brethren, whether in their material or their spiritual affairs. So we must look to the needs of others and work to relieve their pains, to give them rest and to draw them to the spiritual life.

2.3.1.en: Look to the needs of others, for when you show them love you support them and reveal Christ to them, and you are strengthened as you feel the power of Christ working in you and through you, and you are encouraged as you feel your oneness with others, and the blessings of God overflow upon you.

2.4.s.en: (2) The humility and greatness of Christ

2.4.0.en: The mind to which St. Paul refers is the one he had referred to in the preceding verses, namely the mind of humility and denial of self, and it is the mind of Christ Himself, from whom we must learn.

2.5.0.en: "Who, being" is an incorrect Arabic translation; in the original Greek it carries the meaning "who, being and still being," and likewise in English, being in the form of God, and not Was in the form. Accordingly the meaning becomes: He who exists and continues to exist in the divine essential form did not seize or snatch that form for Himself, for He had no need of that, since He is God. That is, He did not try to glorify Himself as God when He became incarnate to redeem us, but He laid aside all His glory and became an ordinary man like us, that is, He took the form of a servant although He is God who fills every place. So He became like us in His humility to save us, but without sin, as we commit it.

2.6.0.en: In Christ's being found in human form, He obeyed the will of the Father, and His obedience reached the utmost degree, for He accepted death on the Cross, although He is the Righteous and Holy One, in order to raise us from death to life.

2.7.0.en: In return for this humility of His, God raised Him to the surpassing glory, and lifted Him up above the highest heavens and seated Him at His right hand, and this applies to the humanity and not the divinity, because the divinity has its glory continuing without interruption.

2.7.1.en: Gave Him a name: in the original Greek, "gave Him the name," that is, the word name is definite, meaning that His full glory appeared above every name and person known in heaven or on earth, because He is God.

2.8.0.en: Jesus means Jehovah saves, and Jehovah is the majestic name that has the greatest holiness among all names, which makes it obligatory for all creatures, heavenly, earthly and under the earth, to offer worship and bowing to Him. This is an expression to indicate the extent of His authority over all, so that every tongue may praise Him and glorify Him, confessing that Christ is the Lord who has all that the Father has of glory.

2.8.1.en: In order that you may have glory in heaven, you must humble yourself at the feet of all, as your Christ humbled Himself and then ascended to His glory in the heavens. In addition, when you humble yourself at the feet of people, you will find Christ beside you washing feet, and you will feel His presence with you and rejoice in His companionship.

2.9.0.en: Therefore, my beloved, as you have walked in obedience to the Gospel, not only during the time I spent among you but all the more in my absence from you in the body, I ask you to strive constantly as long as you are in the body, while you see God before you and fear Him, so that you reject every sin, and even tremble when you fall, and return with repentance and tears, and He has mercy on you.

2.9.1.en: And the word "work out" means continuing the striving throughout life, for salvation is not in a moment but throughout the whole of life, so the fear of God remains in our hearts at all times to keep us away from evil. For as long as we are in the world, the enemy of good will not cease trying to make us fall. So let us beware lest we overcome him today and he strike us down tomorrow.

2.10.0.en: The Spirit of God creates in us spiritual longings and gives us strength to do good, for every good work is a pleasure to the heavenly Father.

2.11.1.en: Disputings: sharp discussion that results in tension.

2.11.2.en: Every good work that you do, do it quietly and without grumbling, which betrays weak love and little patience, and without sharp discussions that create disagreements among you.

2.12.0.en: So that there may be nothing in you deserving reproach and criticism, and that you may be far from all cunning and in a wise Christian simplicity, so that you may be worthy to be children of the heavenly Father, resembling Him in goodness, and live without blemish and have a portion with the ranks of the saints. And because you now live in the midst of a generation that is far from the truth and distorts the truth with cunning, just as the stars guide with their light those who travel in the desert or on the seas, so you shall be like the saints, lights in this age, that those who are far away may be guided by your fragrant conduct.

2.13.0.en: The Apostle asks the people of Philippi to bear witness to the Gospel in their deeds and words, that they may be a cause of boasting for him in the day in which Christ comes to transfer us to His eternal Kingdom, and the reward of his striving and his service to them will be the crowns of heavenly glory.

2.14.0.en: Poured out: the Law of Moses required the pouring out of wine upon the burnt offering presented to God as a sacrifice, and this libation signifies joy. So Paul regards his service and the giving of his life in preaching as if he were being poured out before God to gladden His heart.

2.14.1.en: The sacrifice of your faith: Paul regards the sufferings that the believers in Philippi undergo for holding fast to their faith as if they were offering their lives as a sacrifice before God, and he rejoices in them.

2.14.2.en: The Apostle looks at his life as the libation that the priests of the Old Testament used to place on the sacrifices, borrowing this image to express his striving to draw the Gentiles to the faith, regarding their faith in Christ as a living sacrifice. Just as they accept with joy all the tribulations as a declaration of the sacrifice of their faith, so he also rejoices with them all.

2.15.0.en: Because of this service and its results, which are the source of his joy, he asks them to be also glad and rejoicing with him.

2.15.1.en: Do not be distressed by the multitude of your falls or your weakness or even the coldness of your spiritual feelings, but seek God, who gives you by His Holy Spirit zeal and longings for life with Him and supports you in your striving, in which you persevere to attain the Kingdom. For the grace of God is always with you, and His fear drives sin away from you and makes you grow in the knowledge and love of Him.

2.16.s.en: (4) His sending of Timothy and Epaphroditus

2.16.0.en: St. Paul puts his trust in the Lord that He will arrange the circumstances for sending Timothy to them soon, so that Paul may be gladdened by knowing their news.

2.17.0.en: The Apostle found no one quite like him in love for the people of Philippi and concern for them, because he alone is their spiritual father, at whose hands they believed, and he cares for their shepherding. This is not pride on Paul's part but an expression of the depths of his love. And his sending of Timothy, his son, is as if he himself went to them, because he is his personal representative.

2.18.0.en: All: the false teachers and all who oppose Paul, even among those who preach Christ. All of them seek their own interests and desire from their service their personal glory and not the glorifying of the Lord Jesus in their works, seeking what is their own and not what is the Lord Christ's.

2.19.0.en: Timothy succeeded in all the trials and tribulations to which he had been exposed before, and remained in his humility, emptying himself. He was like a son to St. Paul in the faith, was brought up and trained at his hands, obeyed this father with all faithfulness, and traveled with him everywhere preaching the Gospel.

2.20.0.en: St. Paul decided to send his disciple Timothy as soon as he knew the outcome of the judgment against him, whether the continuation of his imprisonment, or release, or otherwise.

2.21.0.en: St. Paul declares his faith and certainty in the love of the Lord, for he is confident that he too will come to them soon when he is released.

2.22.0.en: In verses 25 to 30 the Apostle speaks about another disciple, Epaphroditus.

2.22.1.en: Although the presence of Epaphroditus in Rome was a help to Paul during his imprisonment there, he preferred to send him to his city, Philippi, so that they might rejoice at meeting him, and this is the obligation of the love that seeks not its own but what is for others.

2.22.2.en: And here St. Paul describes him with several titles that show the extent of Paul's humility, who raises his children to the rank of brotherhood and encourages them and raises them to his own level, making him his partner in service and in preaching the Gospel as a soldier in the army of salvation. Epaphroditus was a delegate from the church of Philippi and carried the love of its people for Paul.

2.23.0.en: Epaphroditus longed for the people of Philippi and was grieved at their grief when they learned that he had been sick, for he was dear to them and beloved by them. The tenderness of feelings appears here, for the people of Philippi were moved by his illness and he was moved by their grief for him.

2.24.0.en: The illness of Epaphroditus was severe, to the point that he was close to death, but God had mercy on him and healed him.

2.24.1.en: And Paul feels that God's mercy was directed to him, because he loves Epaphroditus and depends on him for many services. Paul does not do away with feelings of sorrow when loved ones are sick, because Christianity does not abolish human emotions but elevates them.

2.25.0.en: Less sorrowful: Paul will grieve at the parting from Epaphroditus, but his grief will be less because he will gladden the people of Philippi by their seeing him.

2.25.1.en: St. Paul preferred to give up for a time the service of Epaphroditus to him, and to send him to his own people that they might see him and rejoice in him, so that the Apostle also rejoices in their joy.

2.26.0.en: The Apostle commands them to receive him and honor him for his labor, for he is not fleeing from his service as some might think.

2.27.0.en: Epaphroditus risked his life when he visited Paul in prison, exposing himself to dangers. And although they themselves were not able to come to Rome to visit Paul in prison, Epaphroditus performed his service on their behalf and did not refrain from any service Paul entrusted to him.

2.27.1.en: The illnesses that afflict a person are not the product of chance, but are part of the divine dispensation for our salvation and the proving of our faith. So let us thank the Lord always in every condition, for every condition and in every condition.

2.27.2.en: Spiritual striving and rejecting false teachings
